images.caption: A historical marker in Fayetteville, NC identifying the nearby location of the Fayetteville Arsenal. The Fayetteville Arsenal was a federal military facility used to manufacture, repair, and store military equipment prior to the Civil War. After NC seceded from the Union, it was seized and operated by the Confederacy, until being destroyed by Union troops under the command of Major General William Tecumseh Sherman in March, 1865.
images.alt: A historical marker in Fayetteville, NC identifying the nearby location of the Fayetteville Arsenal. The Fayetteville Arsenal was a federal military facility used to manufacture, repair, and store military equipment prior to the Civil War. After NC seceded from the Union, it was seized and operated by the Confederacy, until being destroyed by Union troops under the command of Major General William Tecumseh Sherman in March, 1865.

images.caption: This sign is located at the back of the parking lot of the Museum of the Cape Fear in Fayetteville, North Carolina. It points visitors to the entrance to Arsenal Park, which is across Martin Luther King Blvd. from the museum and accessible by a walking bridge. This sign is important as it also contains an overview of the history of the site and a diagram showing the layout of the arsenal as it would have appeared before its destruction.

images.filename: Remains of the Fayetteville Arsenal image 1.jpg
images.caption: Little more than foundations remain of the Fayetteville Arsenal in Fayetteville, North Carolina. The facility was destroyed in March of 1865 by Union troops of Major General William Tecumseh Sherman during his army's march through the Carolinas.
images.alt: Little more than foundations remain of the Fayetteville Arsenal in Fayetteville, North Carolina. The facility was destroyed in March of 1865 by Union troops of Major General William Tecumseh Sherman during his army's march through the Carolinas.

images.caption: Though the original towers of the Fayetteville Arsenal, like much of the rest of the facility, are now long-destroyed, the "Ghost Tower" is meant to give visitors a view of the size and shape of the original stone structures.
